title: Greenhouse Gas Auditing
desc: Measure, report and reduce greenhouse gas emissions for an organisation using recognised accounting scopes and data checks.
outcomes: Explain scopes 1, 2 and 3 and emission factors.
Collect activity data and calculate emissions.
Produce an inventory report and reduction plan.
task: Build a greenhouse gas inventory for one small organisation (practice case), with boundary, data, factors, hotspot analysis and reduction plan.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, public emission factors, two peers and a mentor. A practice dataset may be used.
standard: Boundary is stated; each number has unit and source; calculations reproduce; data quality is rated; plan has measurable targets; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Sustainability officers, finance staff, engineers, consultants in training.
evidence: boundary note, data sheet, inventory, hotspot chart, plan
modules: Why measure emissions
Understand
You cannot reduce what you do not count.
Greenhouse gases trap heat; carbon dioxide is the main one, followed by methane and nitrous oxide.
CO2e converts other gases to CO2 equivalent using warming factors.
Reporting supports saving money, customer requests and regulation.
Use recognised methods and keep records.

Methane has a larger warming effect than CO2 per tonne, so a leaking gas line is expressed as tonnes CO2e. Replacing old lights with LEDs saves 2 tonnes CO2e and 20,000 INR a year (an estimate; check your market).
Explain CO2e and a baseline year to a peer.
Peer can explain both terms.
Boundaries and scopes
Understand
Decide what is in and what is out, and write it down.
Organisational boundary by control or ownership.
Scope 1: direct emissions from fuel, vehicles and leaks. Scope 2: purchased electricity, heat and cooling. Scope 3: everything else in the chain.
Record exclusions and reasons.
Keep the boundary the same each year.
Company vehicles are scope 1; electricity is scope 2; business flights and purchased goods are scope 3. A rented warehouse is excluded and the reason is recorded.
Set a boundary for a practice organisation with two inclusions and two exclusions.
Boundary is written and justified.
Collecting activity data
Apply
Good data comes before good calculations.
Sources: bills, meters, fuel logs, travel records and purchase records.
Units must match: litres, kWh, km, kg.
Record source and date; keep invoices.
Fill gaps with clearly labelled estimates.
Fuel invoices give 1,200 litres of diesel. Missing March data is estimated from February and April and flagged as an estimate.
Collect and list data for a practice case with sources.
Every line has unit, source and date.
Emission factors and calculation
Apply
Emissions equal activity data multiplied by an emission factor.
Use recent factors for your country and year and keep the version.
Show each calculation line by line.
Check units and decimal places.
Separate fuels, electricity and refrigerants.
Using example factors (always use current published ones): 1,200 L x 2.68 kg CO2 per litre = 3,216 kg CO2. 40,000 kWh x 0.82 kg CO2e per kWh = 32,800 kg CO2e.
Calculate five lines with a factor table.
Maths and units are correct.
Scope 3 estimates
Analyse
The chain is often the largest part, and the hardest to measure.
Start with the largest categories: purchased goods, travel, commuting, waste.
Use spend-based factors where activity data is unavailable and say so.
Ask the top suppliers for their data.
Improve estimates yearly.
Purchased goods account for 35 per cent of the total using spend factors; commuting 11 per cent and travel 22 per cent.
Estimate two scope 3 categories and rank all categories.
Method stated and ranking shown.
Data quality and checks
Evaluate
Numbers must be trusted.
Reconcile totals with bills and look for outliers.
Check for double counting.
Rate data quality high, medium or low.
Have a second person reproduce one number.
A sample check finds a unit error (MWh entered as kWh) that changes the total by 1,000 times. A duplicated invoice is also removed.
Review a data set and log issues.
At least three checks done and logged.
Hotspots and reduction targets
Analyse
Decide where action pays most.
Rank sources by tonnes.
Estimate tonnes saved per rupee spent for each action.
Set targets with dates and owners.
Track progress quarterly.
Fixing refrigerant leaks saves 6 tonnes CO2e for 15,000 INR; efficient lighting saves 8 per cent for a two-year payback.
Draw a hotspot chart and rank five actions.
Ranking uses tonnes and cost.
Reporting and verification
Create
Share results honestly.
Report summary, method, boundary, exclusions and limits.
Have an independent review where possible.
Update yearly and compare to the baseline.
Publish what you can and keep the evidence.
The report states excluded sources, data quality ratings and the baseline. A peer repeats the diesel calculation and gets the same result.
Write the report and ask a peer to reproduce one number.
Report is reproducible and peer confirmed one number.
quiz: What are scope 1, 2 and 3?
Direct, purchased energy, other chain emissions. (Covered in module 2: Boundaries and scopes. To pass that module: Boundary is written and justified.)
What is CO2e?
CO2 equivalent of other gases. (Covered in module 1: Why measure emissions. To pass that module: Peer can explain both terms.)
Emissions formula?
Activity data x emission factor. (Covered in module 4: Emission factors and calculation. To pass that module: Maths and units are correct.)
Why record sources?
To audit. (Covered in module 3: Collecting activity data. To pass that module: Every line has unit, source and date.)
Name a scope 3 category.
Purchased goods, travel, commuting or waste. (Covered in module 5: Scope 3 estimates. To pass that module: Method stated and ranking shown.)
Double counting?
Counting the same emission twice. (Covered in module 6: Data quality and checks. To pass that module: At least three checks done and logged.)
Why local factors?
Grids and fuels differ. (Covered in module 4: Emission factors and calculation. To pass that module: Maths and units are correct.)
Why state exclusions?
Honesty. (Covered in module 8: Reporting and verification. To pass that module: Report is reproducible and peer confirmed one number.)
How rate data quality?
High, medium, low. (Covered in module 6: Data quality and checks. To pass that module: At least three checks done and logged.)
How often update?
Yearly. (Covered in module 8: Reporting and verification. To pass that module: Report is reproducible and peer confirmed one number.)
rubric: Each emission factor names its source, year and unit
Factors from one consistent set, with any change of set explained
The reporting rule and any threshold for the place are written down
Rule checked on the regulator's page and the report format used

ladder: Why measure emissions

L1: learner can say what CO2e means. Focus module: Why measure emissions (Understand, 3 h). You cannot reduce what you do not count. Key points: Greenhouse gases trap heat; carbon dioxide is the main one, followed by methane and nitrous oxide. CO2e converts other gases to CO2 equivalent using warming factors. Reporting supports saving money, customer requests and regulation. Use recognised methods and keep records.

Teach: open with the worked example. Methane has a larger warming effect than CO2 per tonne, so a leaking gas line is expressed as tonnes CO2e. Replacing old lights with LEDs saves 2 tonnes CO2e and 20,000 INR a year. Then set the activity: Explain CO2e and a baseline year to a peer. Mark against the standard: Peer can explain both terms. Check at this level: What is CO2e? Model answer: CO2 equivalent of other gases.
Boundaries and scopes

L2: learner knows scopes. Focus module: Boundaries and scopes (Understand, 4 h). Decide what is in and what is out, and write it down. Key points: Organisational boundary by control or ownership. Scope 1: direct emissions from fuel, vehicles and leaks. Scope 2: purchased electricity, heat and cooling. Scope 3: everything else in the chain. Record exclusions and reasons. Keep the boundary the same each year.

Teach: open with the worked example. Company vehicles are scope 1; electricity is scope 2; business flights and purchased goods are scope 3. A rented warehouse is excluded and the reason is recorded. Then set the activity: Set a boundary for a practice organisation with two inclusions and two exclusions. Mark against the standard: Boundary is written and justified. Check at this level: What are scope 1, 2 and 3? Model answer: Direct, purchased energy, other chain emissions.
Collecting activity data

L3: learner can collect data. Focus module: Collecting activity data (Apply, 5 h). Good data comes before good calculations. Key points: Sources: bills, meters, fuel logs, travel records and purchase records. Units must match: litres, kWh, km, kg. Record source and date; keep invoices. Fill gaps with clearly labelled estimates.

Teach: open with the worked example. Fuel invoices give 1,200 litres of diesel. Missing March data is estimated from February and April and flagged as an estimate. Then set the activity: Collect and list data for a practice case with sources. Mark against the standard: Every line has unit, source and date. Check at this level: Why record sources? Model answer: To audit.
Emission factors and calculation

L4: learner can calculate. Focus module: Emission factors and calculation (Apply, 5 h). Emissions equal activity data multiplied by an emission factor. Key points: Use recent factors for your country and year and keep the version. Show each calculation line by line. Check units and decimal places. Separate fuels, electricity and refrigerants.

Teach: open with the worked example. Using example factors (always use current published ones): 1,200 L x 2.68 kg CO2 per litre = 3,216 kg CO2. 40,000 kWh x 0.82 kg CO2e per kWh = 32,800 kg CO2e. Scope 3 estimates

L5: learner can find hotspots. Focus module: Scope 3 estimates (Analyse, 5 h). The chain is often the largest part, and the hardest to measure. Key points: Start with the largest categories: purchased goods, travel, commuting, waste. Use spend-based factors where activity data is unavailable and say so. Ask the top suppliers for their data. Improve estimates yearly.

Teach: open with the worked example. Purchased goods account for 35 per cent of the total using spend factors; commuting 11 per cent and travel 22 per cent. Then set the activity: Estimate two scope 3 categories and rank all categories. Mark against the standard: Method stated and ranking shown. Check at this level: Name a scope 3 category. Model answer: Purchased goods, travel, commuting or waste.
Hotspots and reduction targets

L6: learner can lead an inventory. Focus module: Hotspots and reduction targets (Analyse, 4 h). Decide where action pays most. Key points: Rank sources by tonnes. Estimate tonnes saved per rupee spent for each action. Set targets with dates and owners. Track progress quarterly.

Teach: open with the worked example. Fixing refrigerant leaks saves 6 tonnes CO2e for 15,000 INR; efficient lighting saves 8 per cent for a two-year payback. Then set the activity: Draw a hotspot chart and rank five actions. Mark against the standard: Ranking uses tonnes and cost. Check at this level: How do you rank actions to cut emissions? Model answer: By tonnes saved per rupee spent.
Reporting and verification

L7: learner can audit. Focus module: Reporting and verification (Create, 4 h). Share results honestly. Key points: Report summary, method, boundary, exclusions and limits. Have an independent review where possible. Update yearly and compare to the baseline. Publish what you can and keep the evidence.

Teach: open with the worked example. The report states excluded sources, data quality ratings and the baseline. A peer repeats the diesel calculation and gets the same result. Then set the activity: Write the report and ask a peer to reproduce one number. Mark against the standard: Report is reproducible and peer confirmed one number.
